1.title: A Jealous and Avenging God
1.context: The book is addressed to one city: the burden against Nineveh, the book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite. After this line the prophet never appears again. The book opens with God's character, and its first claim joins what readers often separate: jealous and avenging, taking vengeance on His foes.
1.question: Which half of this portrait of God have you been tempted to keep, and which half to quietly drop?

1.title: Slow to Anger, Great in Power
1.context: In the same poem, God is slow to anger and great in power, and He will by no means leave the guilty unpunished. Between Jonah's mercy to Nineveh and this book's sentence lie generations; the text itself measures the patience in years of Assyrian cruelty borne by other nations.
1.question: Where has God's slowness to anger been a mercy in your life rather than an absence?

1.title: Who Can Stand His Indignation?
1.context: The theophany: sea rebuked and dried, Bashan and Carmel withered, mountains quaking and hills melting, rocks shattered before wrath poured out like fire. The questions at the end are not answered; they are left ringing.
1.question: What happens to your prayer life when you let God be this large before you ask Him for anything?

1.title: A Stronghold in the Day of Distress
1.context: The comfort center: the LORD is good, a stronghold in the day of distress; He cares for those who trust in Him. Against Nineveh the same chapter promises an overwhelming flood and an end of plotting; affliction will not rise up a second time. The plotter who comes from Nineveh is never named in the text.
1.question: Who needs to hear from you this week that God is a stronghold in the day of distress, not only a judge of the guilty?

1.title: I Will Afflict You No Longer
1.context: The chapter turns fully to Judah: though the enemy is allied and numerous, they will be cut down; the yoke is broken and the shackles torn away. Nineveh is promised a grave and no descendants to carry her name. The messenger's feet on the mountains (1:15) stand in Isaiah 52:7 in nearly the same words; each book tells it whole in its own place.
1.question: What yoke in your life has God already announced an end to, that you still carry as if it were permanent?

2.title: Guard the Fortress
2.context: The fall is narrated as scene: a scatterer advances, and the commands to guard, watch, brace, and summon strength are spoken to a city that cannot use them. Verse 2 turns mid-battle to Jacob's restoration, a seam the retelling leaves standing; the battle is the comfort.
2.question: What strength have you been summoning that God is asking you to stop trusting?

2.title: Chariots Like Torches
2.context: The attacking force is described in color and speed: red shields, scarlet warriors, chariot fittings flashing like fire, chariots dashing like torches and darting like lightning through streets and plazas already inside the city.
2.question: Where have you discovered that the threat you guarded the road against was already inside the walls?

2.title: The River Gates Are Open
2.context: Nineveh's nobles stumble as they race to the wall. The shortest sentence of the fall follows: the river gates are thrown open and the palace collapses. The city's decree is exile, the fate it dealt to nations, carried out in its own grammar.
2.question: What collapse in your life turned out to be a decree you needed rather than only a disaster?

2.title: Plunder the Silver
2.context: Nineveh is a pool draining away; officers cry for the fleeing to stop and no one turns back. The silver and gold stored from centuries of plunder is plundered in turn, and the city is emptied, desolate, hearts melting and faces pale.
2.question: What pool in your life is draining that you keep shouting at to stop?

2.title: Where Is the Lions’ Lair?
2.context: Assyria's kings pictured their empire as a lion's den filled with mauled prey for its cubs. The prophet walks the den and asks where it is. The chapter ends with God speaking in the first person: Behold, I am against you; the prey is cut off from the earth, and the messengers' voices are heard no more.
2.question: What den have you filled with prey that God may be walking through with this question?

3.title: Woe to the City of Blood
3.context: The third chapter reads the charges under the funeral word woe: city of blood, full of lies, full of plunder, never without prey. The assault is heard before it is seen: the crack of the whip, the rumble of the wheel, galloping horse and bounding chariot.
3.question: What title would the charges against your own city, your own house, read if they were read aloud?

3.title: Dead Bodies Without End
3.context: One verse of carnage, told in the text's own terms and left there: charging horseman, flashing sword, heaps of slain, corpses stumbled over. The chapter hurries past the bodies to the reason for them.
3.question: How do you keep from going numb when the text, or the news, stacks suffering faster than you can grieve it?

3.title: I Will Make a Spectacle of You
3.context: The charge is figured as a harlot who betrayed nations by her prostitution and clans by her witchcraft: an empire run on seduction, treaties, trade, and sorcery, drawing peoples in to betray them. The sentence is exposure before those same nations, and the book's refrain stands a second time: Behold, I am against you.
3.question: What in your life has been built on seduction, drawing people in with less than the truth?

3.title: Are You Better Than Thebes?
3.context: The precedent is argued like a decided case. Thebes stood by the Nile with water for a rampart and a wall, and Cush, Egypt, Put, and Libya as her strength and allies. Nineveh is asked to name one advantage Thebes did not have in greater measure.
3.question: What fallen example has God already placed in front of you as your precedent and your warning?

3.title: She Went into Captivity
3.context: Thebes fell anyway: exile, captivity, lots cast for her dignitaries, nobles bound in chains, and her infants dashed to pieces at the head of every street, told in one line because the text tells it in one line. The precedent closes the case against Nineveh.
3.question: What makes you believe your walls, your allies, or your record exempt you from a precedent like this?

4.title: Figs into the Mouth of the Eater
4.context: The verdict crosses over with two words: you too. Nineveh will go into hiding like Thebes, and her fortresses are ripe figs on shaken trees, falling into the mouth of the eater; they do not need to be stormed, only shaken.
4.question: Which of your defenses would fall with a shaking rather than a siege?

4.title: Repair the Brick Kiln
4.context: The troops are taunted, the land's gates stand open with their bars burned, and the siege preparations are mocked in orders: draw water, work the clay, repair the brick kiln. At the kiln itself, fire and sword are already waiting; multiplication only makes more locusts.
4.question: What frantic preparing are you doing for a battle God says will be decided another way?

4.title: Locusts on the Wall
4.context: The empire's own people are its locusts: merchants more than the stars, stripping the land and flying away; guards and scribes settled on the walls only while the day is cold, gone when the sun rises, no one knowing where.
4.question: Who around you is settled only while things are cold, and what will the sunrise show?

4.title: Scattered with No One to Gather
4.context: The king of Assyria, never named in the book, is addressed by his office at the end: his shepherds slumber, his officers sleep, and his people are scattered on the mountains with no one to gather them. Micah prayed for a Shepherd to gather Israel; for Assyria the scattering is final.
4.question: Who has God placed in your care that depends on you being awake?

4.title: No Healing for Your Injury
4.context: The book closes on the wound: no healing for the injury, and all who hear the news applauding the downfall, for who has not experienced Nineveh's constant cruelty. It is the last sound in Nahum, and the retelling ends on it as the book does.
4.question: What wound are you still asking God to heal that He may instead be asking you to stop reopening?
